About: Lorentz Boost vs Euclidean Rotation

Source

Lecture
10 — Lorentz transformations (Minkowski metric · inertial frames · Lorentz transformations).
Simulation
Simulation 2 — Lorentz transformation vs Euclidean rotation (guided inquiry).
Concept
A Lorentz boost is a hyperbolic rotation in spacetime that preserves the invariant hyperbola −(ct)²+x²=−1, just as an ordinary rotation preserves the circle x²+y²=1 — but the two transformations differ in how their axes move.
Serves
Interpret Lorentz transformations as hyperbolic rotations; identify invariant quantities under Lorentz transformations; describe Minkowski spacetime and its metric structure.
Inquiry
What angle do the rotated axes keep? Do the boosted axes stay perpendicular? Which quantities stay fixed as θ and v/c change?
Misconception
"A Lorentz boost is just a rotation, so the primed axes stay perpendicular." (Encoded as prediction choice A.)

Guided Inquiry

1 · Two ways to change coordinates

Take a moment with the two panels. On the left is the x–y plane, where a rotation through θ carries the axes x and y to new axes x′ and y′. On the right is the ct–x plane of spacetime with c = 1, where a boost to a frame moving at v/c carries ct and x to ct′ and x′. Those dashed 45° lines on the right are the paths of light.

2 · What the boosted axes do

Let’s start simple. Both panels begin with the primed axes lying right on top of the unprimed ones. Now imagine raising v/c from 0 — what do you think ct′ and x′ will do?

Have a look at the last row of the strip under each panel: it reports the angle between that panel’s own primed axes, ∠(x′, y′) on the left and ∠(ct′, x′) on the right.

3 · The curve a boost preserves

Now for the shapes. A rotation leaves x² + y² unchanged, so a point can only slide around a circle. A boost leaves −(ct)² + x² unchanged instead. So what do you think — along what curve does event E₂ slide as v/c changes?

4 · How far the axes can close

Now let’s push the boost as far as it can go. θ can be increased without limit, coming back round every 360°. The boost parameter is the rapidity φ, with v/c = tanh φ, and φ is unbounded too. So as φ grows, what do you think ∠(ct′, x′) does?

And here’s a neat bonus: γ is cosh φ, just as v/c is tanh φ — at v/c = 0.80 the γ readout shows 1.667 = cosh(1.0986).

5 · One sign, two geometries

Let’s put the two side by side. A rotation mixes x with y using cos and sin and preserves x² + y²: a circle. A boost mixes ct with x using cosh and sinh and preserves −(ct)² + x²: a hyperbola. That one minus sign is the whole difference.

It’s also why the boosted axes close in on the light line instead of staying perpendicular — and so why simultaneity belongs to a frame, not to the events themselves.

Try it for yourself: ◯ Invariant curves draws the circle and the hyperbolae, and ⚛︎ The Physics has the matrices whenever you want them.

Read the symbols

▾
  • θ = rotation angle (left panel), 0°–80°.
  • γ = 1/√(1−(v/c)²), the Lorentz factor.
  • black axes = unprimed frame (x, y / x, ct).
  • orange axes = primed frame (x′, y′ / x′, ct′).
  • teal curve = the invariant (circle / hyperbolas), when Invariant curves is on.
  • dashed = the light cone ct = ±x.

The circle uses cos/sin; the hyperbola uses cosh/sinh: that is why one is a "circular" and the other a "hyperbolic" rotation.

Euclidean rotation

Both axes rotate the same way by θ → they stay perpendicular. The preserved set is the circle.

Lorentz boost (c = 1)

ct′ tilts toward x and x′ tilts toward ct, each by arctan(v/c) → they scissor. The preserved set is a pair of hyperbolas.

How the axes differ & the invariant interval

Signature (−, +): ds² = −(c dt)² + dx² (timelike is negative, spacelike is positive). Unit ticks sit where the invariant curves meet each primed axis: the ct′-axis intersects the timelike hyperbola −(ct)²+x² = −1, while the x′-axis intersects the spacelike hyperbola −(ct)²+x² = +1. Both curves are drawn in teal when Invariant curves is on. On the left, circle ticks are evenly spaced. On the right, hyperbola ticks spread apart because the Minkowski metric is not Euclidean.

The Physics

Lorentz boost vs Euclidean rotation · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

The sim puts a Euclidean rotation of the x–y plane next to a Lorentz boost of the ct–x plane, with c = 1. Both change coordinates by turning a pair of axes, and setting them side by side shows what the two have in common and where they part.

What you'll learn

  • What it means to relabel one fixed point with a second set of axes.
  • How each transformation changes the angle between its primed axes.
  • Which combination of coordinates each one leaves unchanged.
  • How v/c, γ and the rapidity φ are related.
Each panel starts with its primed axes lying on the unprimed ones (θ = 0, v/c = 0).

What's on screen

  • Unprimed axes (grey): x and y on the left, x and ct on the right, with unit ticks at 1 and 2.
  • Primed axes (amber): x′ and y′ on the left, x′ and ct′ on the right.
  • Light cone (dashed yellow, right panel): the lines ct = ±x.
  • Sample points P₁, P₂ (left) and events E₁, E₂ (right), with dashed lines down to the primed axes.
  • Invariant curves (teal) and the amber primed grid and ticks, when their buttons are on.
  • Strip under each panel: the points in both coordinate systems, an invariant row, and the angle between the primed axes.
See itReturn both panels to their start, with the sample points and strips showing. Watch for: the amber axes lying exactly on the grey ones, and the strips listing P₁, P₂ and E₁, E₂.

03

A boost tilts both axes toward the light line

Both panels relabel one fixed point with a second set of axes; only the axes move. Take c = 1 and write β = v/c. The primed frame moves at v along +x relative to the unprimed one.

Rotation: x′ = x cos θ + y sin θ,   y′ = −x sin θ + y cos θ
Boost: ct′ = γ(ct − βx),   x′ = γ(x − βct),   γ = 1/√(1 − β²)
The sim at θ = 39° and v/c = 0.80. Angles are measured on the diagram, with ct and x on equal scales.
  • Left. x′ and y′ turn the same way through θ, so ∠(x′, y′) = 90° at every θ.
  • Right. The ct′ axis is the line x = βct and the x′ axis is the line ct = βx. Each tilts by arctan β, ct′ toward x and x′ toward ct, so the pair closes on the light line: ∠(ct′, x′) = 90° − 2 arctan β.
  • At v/c = 0.80 each axis tilts 38.7° and ∠(ct′, x′) = 12.7°.
  • The x′ axis is every event with ct′ = 0: the events the primed observer calls simultaneous with the origin.
See itSet θ = 39° and v/c = 0.80, with the readouts on. Watch for: ∠(x′, y′) = 90.0° under the left panel and ∠(ct′, x′) = 12.7° under the right, with the two amber axes on the right leaning together.
04

Each transformation preserves one combination

A fixed point gets new coordinates, but one combination of them stays the same. A rotation keeps x² + y², so the point lies on a circle. A boost keeps −(ct)² + x², so the event lies on a hyperbola.

One sign separates the circle from the hyperbola.
  • The interval. The sim writes it as s² = −(ct)² + x²: negative inside the light cone (timelike), positive outside (spacelike).
  • Hyperbola. −(ct)² + x² = −1 has the light lines as asymptotes. E₂ sits at (x, ct) = (0.89, 1.34) on it, and its invariant row reads −1.00 at every v/c. The sim also draws −(ct)² + x² = +1.
  • Ticks. A primed unit tick sits where its axis meets its curve. On the circle it stays 1 from the origin. On the hyperbola it moves outward: at v/c = 0.80 it is γ√(1 + β²) = 2.13 from the origin on the page.
See itDraw the invariant curves, the primed grid and the ticks at θ = 39° and v/c = 0.80. Watch for: a teal circle on the left and teal hyperbolae on the right, each amber tick on its curve, and both invariant rows reading 1.00 → 1.00 on the left and −1.00 → −1.00 on the right.
05

The axes close without reaching the light line

The angle between the boosted axes follows arctan, not a straight line. From v/c = 0.40 to 0.80 it falls from 46.4° to 12.7°, while γ rises from 1.091 to 1.667.

θ v/c

These are the sim's own θ and v/c sliders.

  • Rapidity. The parameter φ is defined by v/c = tanh φ, and then γ = cosh φ. The panel above shows φ = artanh(v/c).
  • The slider stops at v/c = 0.80, where φ = 1.10 and each axis is still 6.3° from the light line.
  • The angle reaches 0° only at v/c = 1. Since tanh φ stays below 1 at every finite φ, the axes approach the light line and never lie on it.
v/c = tanh φ. The slider stops at the first marked point.
See itRun v/c = 0.40 and then v/c = 0.80, one after the other. Watch for: ∠(ct′, x′) reading 46.4° and then 12.7°, which is not half, with the axes at 0.80 still apart from the light line.
06

A boost is a rotation through the rapidity

Put γ = cosh φ and β = tanh φ. The boost matrix then has the form of a rotation, with cosh and sinh in place of cos and sin. Lecture 10 calls this parameter ζ; the sim and this sheet call it φ.

The sim's boost matrix at c = 1.
  • Rapidities add. Two boosts in the same direction make one boost of φ₁ + φ₂, as two rotations add their angles. Two boosts of v/c = 0.50 have φ = 0.549 each, so φ = 1.099 and v/c = tanh 1.099 = 0.80, not 1.00.
  • Light-cone form. A boost only rescales ct + x by e−φ and ct − x by e+φ, and the two factors cancel in −(ct)² + x².
  • No period. θ repeats every 360°, but cosh and sinh never repeat, so a boost never returns the axes to where they started.
  • E₂ is at rapidity 0.80, (x, ct) = (sinh 0.80, cosh 0.80). A boost φ gives it rapidity 0.80 − φ, so at v/c = tanh 0.80 = 0.664 it lies on the ct′ axis.
The boost in light-cone coordinates.
See itSet v/c = 0.66, the slider step nearest 0.664, with the events on. Watch for: E₂'s boosted coordinates reading about (x′, ct′) = (0.01, 1.00), so E₂ sits on the ct′ axis.
07

Where it matters

  • Everyday speeds. An airliner at 250 m/s has v/c = 8.3 × 10⁻⁷. Each axis tilts by 0.17 arcsec and γ − 1 = 3.5 × 10⁻¹³, so the axes look square.
  • Cosmic-ray muons at v/c ≈ 0.998 have γ ≈ 15.8 and φ ≈ 3.45, far past this slider. In the ground frame γ stretches their lifetime, which is why many reach the ground.
  • LHC protons at 6.5 TeV have γ ≈ 6930 and φ ≈ 9.5. ∠(ct′, x′) is about 0.002 arcsec, and the protons still move slower than light.
Go deeper: the low-speed limit
  • For v/c ≪ 1, γ ≈ 1 and the boost becomes x′ ≈ x − vt and t′ ≈ t − vx/c². The second term is the only trace of relativity, and it is negligible at everyday speeds.
08

Summary

In one line. A rotation keeps x² + y² and a right angle between its axes; a boost keeps −(ct)² + x² and closes its axes toward the light line without reaching it.

Key points

  • Both panels relabel a fixed point. The rotation keeps ∠(x′, y′) = 90° and x² + y².
  • The boost tilts ct′ and x′ by arctan(v/c) each, so ∠(ct′, x′) = 90° − 2 arctan(v/c), and it keeps −(ct)² + x².
  • γ = cosh φ and v/c = tanh φ. Rapidities add, and v/c stays below 1.

Common mix-ups

  • "A boost is a rotation, so the primed axes stay perpendicular." Only ∠(x′, y′) stays 90°. On the page the boosted axes close up, and they remain orthogonal only in the spacetime sense that carries the minus sign.
  • "Only ct′ tilts." Both axes tilt by arctan(v/c). The tilt of x′ is the frame's own simultaneity.
  • "Push v/c high enough and the axes land on the light line." v/c = tanh φ stays below 1, so they only approach it.

Things to try on your own

  • Turn on the grid and the invariant curves, raise v/c from 0 to 0.80, and follow the amber tick on ct′ along its hyperbola.
  • Work out by hand the v/c at which ∠(ct′, x′) = 45° (√2 − 1 ≈ 0.41), then set the slider and read the strip.
  • At v/c = 0.50, compute γ and φ by hand (1.155, 0.549) and check them against the live panel in section 05.
